title: Microstructural Refinement in a Low Alloy High Strength Martensitic Steel
abstract: Abstract The prior austenite grain (PAG) size of a low alloy high strength martensitic steel, AF9628, was refined by rapid austenitizing heat treatments at 825 and 850 °C. The reduction in PAG size of as high as 97% was obtained. After one rapid austenitizing cycle, the newly nucleated (small) PAGs were observed to be preferentially located at the prior austenite grain boundaries of starting microstructure, although a small number of fine PAGs were also observed in the interior of PAGs of starting microstructure. A more uniform distribution of fine PAGs was observed with an increase in the number of cycles. The average number of austenite nucleation sites in a given area was 43.4% higher at 850 °C than 825 °C after one cycle. A higher nucleation rate at 850 °C resulted in a smaller PAG size at this temperature than 825 °C after one and four cycles. A higher growth rate at 850 °C resulted in a larger PAG size at this temperature than 825 °C after sixteen cycles. Prior studies have discussed the role of growth rate in microstructure evolution during rapid austenitizing heat treatments at different temperatures and not the role of nucleation rate, which is discussed for the first time in current study. Furthermore, the X-ray diffraction results indicated a higher amount of retained austenite in the finest microstructure and it can affect the strength in these microstructures. This aspect of microstructure evolution is also not reported in prior studies on microstructural refinement with rapid austenitizing method.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Microstructural refinement of martensitic steels has potential to impart superior mechanical properties, including strength and toughness [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. The microstructure can be refined with thermomechanical processing, including high temperature equal-channel angular pressing [ 4 ]. In many applications, it is necessary or desirable to refine the microstructure with heat treatments only, without recourse to mechanical processing. In this study, the microstructure of a low alloy high strength martensitic steel was refined only with heat treatments.

Grange first reported the refinement of martensitic or tempered martensitic microstructures in several different steels by a rapid austenitizing heat treatment, which consists of rapidly heating through the  A 1  to  A 3  temperature range, limiting the maximum temperature to the minimum required for complete austenitization, and immediately quenching [ 1 ]. Further microstructural refinement was reported from two or more cycles of rapid austenitizing heat treatment [ 1 ]. In a more recent study [ 2 ], Hidalgo and Santofimia reported martensitic microstructure refinement in Fe−0.3C–1.6Si–3.5Mn steel by rapid austenitizing heat treatments. The approach of rapid austenitizing heat treatments was employed in the current study to refine the martensitic microstructure in AF9628 steel.

The mechanisms of microstructural refinement have been discussed in prior studies [ 5 ,  6 ] suggesting that rapid austenitizing heat treatments essentially consist of nucleation of austenite grains at a temperature slightly above  A 3  and their limited growth due to a short hold time. This sequence of phase transformations from martensite to austenite on heating above  A 3  and back to martensite on quenching continues in each subsequent rapid austenitizing cycle, which results in a higher level of microstructural refinement with the number of cycles. However, the  relative  importance of different boundaries in a martensitic microstructure, specifically prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs) versus intragranular (e.g., packet or block) boundaries, to act as the nucleation sites for austenite is not fully understood. Further, the mechanisms by which the specific heat treatment temperatures above the  A 3  temperature affects the microstructure evolution are not discussed in prior studies. Moreover, prior studies describe both nucleation of austenite grains and their growth as affecting the final microstructure after rapid austenitizing heat treatments. However, the relative contributions of nucleation and growth as a function of heat treatment temperature or number of rapid austenitizing cycles are not elucidated in previous reports.

In this study, a systematic set of rapid austenitizing experiments was conducted at two different temperatures above  A 3  and the number of rapid austenitizing cycles was varied in the range 1 to 16. The microstructural characterizations were conducted via electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) method in a scanning electron microscope. The EBSD data and maps were analyzed in detail to evaluate the relative importance of different boundaries in acting as the nucleation sites for austenite on rapid heating. The experiments at two different temperatures permitted an elucidation of the mechanisms of microstructure evolution, especially the effects of specific heat treatment temperatures above the  A 3  temperature on nucleation rates of austenite grains and the resultant mechanisms of microstructure refinement. The number of austenite nucleation sites was quantified in the microstructures after rapid austenitizing heat treatments at the two temperatures to elucidate the relative contributions of nucleation and growth in determining the final microstructure. The relative effects of nucleation and growth on microstructure as a function of number of rapid austenitizing cycles were also assessed.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
paragraphs: The material for this study was taken from a 101.6-mm-diameter bar of wrought AF9628 steel. The chemical composition of material was reported previously [ 7 ] and is shown in Table  1 . sections.heading: Phase Transformation Temperatures
paragraphs: A sample from the wrought bar of AF9628 was characterized with differential thermal analysis (DTA) at the heating rate of 0.5 °C/s to determine the  A 1  and  A 3  phase transformation temperatures for this steel. To assess the phase transformation temperatures with an independent approach, a magnet was placed on top of the differential thermal analysis unit before the start of experiment, which permitted the weight change to be recorded during heating due to martensite/ferrite (ferromagnetic) → austenite (paramagnetic) phase transformation. A similar approach to detect temperature-dependent magnetic transitions in a martensitic stainless steel was employed in a prior study [ 8 ]. The results from differential thermal analysis experiments are shown in Fig.  1  and will be discussed later. The  A 1  and  A 3  phase transformation temperatures were also estimated with CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) method using Pandat™ (CompuTherm LLC, Middleton, WI, USA) software with the PanFe 2018 database. Fig. 1 Results from differential thermal analysis of AF9628 Steel at the heating rate of 0.5 °C/s. ( a ) Temperature difference versus temperature plot, and ( b ) weight versus temperature plot. A magnet was placed on the top of differential thermal analysis equipment, which caused the weight change to be registered during heating due to martensite/ferrite (ferromagnetic) to austenite (paramagnetic) phase transformation

sections.heading: Heat Treatment and Characterization of Starting Microstructure for Rapid Austenitizing Experiments
paragraphs: An approximately 25.4-mm-thick slice was sectioned from the as-received bar by band saw and then sectioned by wire electrical discharge machining (EDM) into four quarter–round blocks, each of thickness of approximately 25.4 mm, for heat treatment. One block was austenitized at 1010 °C for 1.1 hours and quenched in water (Fig.  2 a). A sample from the quenched block was metallographically prepared, and its microstructure was characterized in a scanning electron microscope (SEM) with automated scans using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). An area of approximately 1 mm × 1 mm was characterized at a step size of 0.5 μm using a combination of beam control scans and automated stage movements [ 9 ]. The individual tiles of EBSD data were combined to produce a seamless image by means of the open-source software AnyStitch [ 10 ]. The EBSD data were cleaned with a neighbor confidence index (CI) correlation method (minimum CI = 0.2), and an orientation map was plotted using TSL OIM Analysis software (supplier: TexSEM Laboratories, Inc., Draper, UT, USA). The PAGBs were delineated in the EBSD map using a misorientation thresholding method for misorientations in the ranges 19°–48° and 61°–62.8°. The misorientation thresholding method of delineating PAGBs is described in prior studies [ 2 ,  11 ,  12 ]. Fig. 2 Schematic of the heat treatments employed in current study. ( a ) Austenitizing at 1010 °C for 1.1 hours, followed by water quench, ( b ) one rapid austenitizing cycle consisting of heating at the rate of 10 °C/s to 825 or 850 °C for 30 s, followed by brine quench, and ( c ) austenitizing at 825 °C for 1 hour, followed by water quench

sections.heading: Rapid Austenitizing Heat Treatments and Characterization of Refined Microstructures
paragraphs: The material after heat treatment schedule of Fig.  2 a and with EBSD map shown in Fig.  3  was the starting microstructure for rapid austenitizing experiments to refine the microstructure in this study. The specimens with nominal dimensions of 12 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm were sectioned from austenitized and quenched block (i.e., heat-treated per the schedule shown in Fig.  2 a) for rapid austenitizing heat treatments. One rapid austenitizing heat treatment cycle consisted of rapidly heating at the rate of approximately 10 °C/s from room temperature to a temperature (825 or 850 °C) slightly above  A 3 , holding for 30 s, and quenching in brine (Fig.  2 b). The rapid heating was conducted in air using an induction furnace. The rapid austenitizing heat treatments were performed for 1, 4, and 16 cycles at both the temperatures (i.e., 825 and 850 °C). The microstructures of AF9628 steel after rapid austenitizing heat treatments were characterized in an SEM using automated EBSD scans at the step size of 0.05 μm. A small step size was used for microstructures generated by rapid austenitizing heat treatments to collect data with sufficient statistics from fine microstructural features. The EBSD data were cleaned with a neighbor CI correlation method (minimum CI = 0.2), and an orientation map was plotted using TSL OIM Analysis software. The PAGBs were delineated in the EBSD maps of rapidly austenitized materials using the misorientation thresholding method for misorientations in the ranges 19°–48° and 61°–62.8°, which was similar to the method described above for the starting (coarse) microstructure. Fig. 3 Microstructure of the material after austenitizing at 1010 °C for 1.1 hours, followed by water quench. The PAGBs are delineated as white lines for misorientations in the ranges 19°–48° and 61–62.8°

sections.heading: Heat Treatment at Low Austenitizing Temperature and Characterization of Microstructure
paragraphs: The material after heat treatment schedule of Fig.  2 a and with EBSD map shown in Fig.  3  was also heat treated at a low austenitizing temperature of 825 °C without employing rapid heating. The hold time at 825 °C was 1 hour, which was followed by quenching in water (Fig.  2 c). The heating rates depicted in Fig.  2 a, c were similar, whereas the heating rate depicted in Fig.  2 b was faster that was achieved in an induction furnace as described in Section " Rapid Austenitizing Heat Treatments and Characterization of Refined Microstructures ."

The microstructure of heat-treated material (per the schedule shown in Fig.  2 a followed by Fig.  2 c) was characterized in an SEM with automated scans using EBSD at a step size of 0.5 μm using the methodology described above for starting microstructure in Section " Heat Treatment and Characterization of Starting Microstructure for Rapid Austenitizing Experiments ." The EBSD data were cleaned with a neighbor CI correlation method (minimum CI = 0.2), and an orientation map was plotted using TSL OIM Analysis software. The PAGBs were delineated in the EBSD map using a misorientation thresholding method for misorientations in the ranges 19°–48° and 61°–62.8°.

sections.heading: Average Prior Austenite Grain Size Measurements
paragraphs: The prior austenite grain (PAG) size measurements were conducted on the EBSD maps, where the PAGBs were delineated by the misorientation thresholding method. A grid of horizontal and vertical lines was overlaid on the EBSD maps, and the intersections of the gridlines with PAGBs were counted to determine the average size of PAGs using the procedure outlined in reference [ 13 ]. This method of measuring average PAG size has been utilized in prior publications [ 11 ,  12 ].

sections.heading: Quantification of Austenite Nucleation Sites in EBSD Maps
paragraphs: The newly nucleated (i.e., small) prior austenite grains in EBSD maps of rapidly austenitized materials were quantified using FIJI, which is an open-source software package for processing and analyzing images [ 14 ]. The boundaries of small PAGs were traced, and areas of individual newly nucleated PAGs were measured. The areas of all small PAGs were added to calculate the area fraction of newly nucleated PAGs in a given EBSD map. The number of traced (small) PAGs in EBSD maps was counted to quantify the number of austenite nucleation sites during a particular rapid austenitizing heat treatment.

sections.heading: X-ray Diffraction Experiments
paragraphs: The samples for characterizations by X-ray diffraction (XRD) were prepared with standard metallographic procedures to a final surface finish of 1 μm with diamond paste. The phases present in the starting and refined microstructures were characterized with XRD using Cu– K α  radiation. The background was subtracted from the XRD patterns, and the contributions from Cu– K α2  wavelength were also removed from the patterns. Therefore, the processed data consisted of diffracted beam intensities only from the Cu– K α1  wavelength (i.e., 1.5406 Å).

sections.heading: Microhardness Measurements
paragraphs: The microhardness for different microstructures was measured with a Vickers indenter with a force of 1000 gf and a dwell time of 10 s per ASTM E92-17 [ 15 ].

sections.heading: Phase Transformation Temperatures
paragraphs: The results from differential thermal analysis experiments for AF9628 steel are presented in Fig.  1 . The results indicate that the  A 1  and  A 3  phase transformation temperatures are 714 and 803 °C, respectively (Fig.  1 a). The weight as a function of temperature is plotted in Fig.  1 b, which shows that a rapid increase in weight starts at 743 °C that agrees well with the valley in the  ΔT  versus  T  curve (Fig.  1 a). The weight stabilizes at temperatures above 766 °C, which agrees well with the Curie temperature of 770 °C for low C steels.

Thermodynamic simulation with Pandat™ predicts  A 1  and  A 3  temperatures to be 755  and 810 °C, respectively. A comparison of experimental results and model predictions indicates a good agreement in  A 3  temperature, while there is a mismatch in  A 1  temperature (Table  2 ). Table 2 Comparison of experimental result and model prediction for phase transformation temperatures ( A 1  and  A 3 ) Phase transformation temperatures Experimental (DTA) results at the heating rate of  0.5 °C/s Thermodynamic model prediction (PANDAT) A 1  (°C) 714 755 A 3  (°C) 803 810
The experiments in a dilatometer on this material indicated the martensite start ( M s ) and the martensite finish ( M f ) temperatures of 380 and 101 °C, respectively [ 16 ].

sections.heading: Microstructures after Different Heat Treatments
paragraphs: The EBSD orientation map of the material after austenitizing at 1010 °C and water quenching (per the schedule in Fig.  2 a) is shown in Fig.  3 , where PAGBs are shown as white boundaries.

The microstructures after rapid austenitizing heat treatments at different temperatures and number of cycles are presented in Fig.  4 . Several small PAGs were observed at the PAGBs of starting microstructure (i.e., Fig.  3 ) after one cycle at 825 °C, although the microstructure still contained large PAGs (Fig.  4 a). The size of small PAGs decreases and a larger fraction of material contains small PAGs after four cycles at 825 °C (Fig.  4 b) compared to one cycle at 825 °C (Fig.  4 a). A uniform distribution of small PAGs and no large PAGs were observed after sixteen cycles at 825 °C (Fig.  4 c). Several small PAGs were observed at the PAGBs of starting microstructure (i.e., Fig.  3 ) after one cycle at 850 °C, although the microstructure still contained large PAGs (Fig.  4 d), which is similar to the microstructure after one cycle at 825 °C (Fig.  4 a). The material consisted of small and medium PAGs after four cycles at 850 °C (Fig.  4 e). Further, no large PAGs were observed after four cycles at 850 °C, which contrasts with the microstructure after four cycles at 825 °C (Fig.  4 b). A uniform distribution of small PAGs was observed after sixteen cycles at 850 °C (Fig.  4 f). However, the PAGs appear coarser than in the microstructure after sixteen cycles at 825 °C (Fig.  4 c). Fig. 4 Microstructure of AF9628 steel after rapid austenitizing heat treatments. ( a ) 1 cycle at 825 °C, (b) 4 cycles at 825 °C, ( c ) 16 cycles at 825 °C, ( d ) 1 cycle at 850 °C, ( e ) 4 cycles at 850 °C, and (f) 16 cycles at 850 °C. The PAGBs are delineated as white lines for misorientations in the ranges 19°–48° and 61°–62.8°

The EBSD orientation map of the examined steel after austenitizing at 825 °C for 1 hour and water quenching (per the schedule in Fig.  2 a followed by Fig.  2 c) is shown in Fig.  5 , where PAGBs are shown as white boundaries. Fig. 5 Microstructure of the examined steel after austenitizing at 825 °C for 1 hour, followed by water quench. The PAGBs are delineated as white lines for misorientations in the ranges 19°–48° and 61°–62.8°

sections.heading: Quantification of Austenite Nucleation Sites
paragraphs: The individual newly nucleated (small) PAGs in the EBSD maps after one rapid austenitizing cycle at the two temperatures were identified and counted (Fig.  7 ). In the scan area shown in Fig.  7 a for the heat treatment temperature of 825 °C, the number of austenite nucleation site was 106. In the scan area shown in Fig.  7 c for the heat treatment temperature of 850 °C, the number of austenite nucleation site was 137. This corresponds to an average number of nucleation sites after one rapid austenitizing cycle in a fixed analysis area of 1000 μm 2  of 5.4 and 7.8 at 825 °C and 850 °C, respectively (Table  4 ). Therefore, the average number of nucleation sites in a fixed area was 43.4% higher at 850 °C than 825 °C. The area fraction of newly nucleated PAGs was 0.253 and 0.387 at 825 °C and 850 °C, respectively (Table  4 ). Thus, the area fraction of newly nucleated PAGs was 53.2% higher at 850 °C than 825 °C. sections.heading: Misorientation Angle Distributions
paragraphs: As described previously [ 11 ,  12 ], the martensite variant boundaries within prior austenite grains (i.e., packet, block and sub-block boundaries) have misorientation angles less than 19° or in the range 48°–61° in this steel. To assess the relative distributions of misorientation angle for PAGBs and martensite variant boundaries within PAGs in different heat-treated conditions, these distributions were plotted for different microstructures (Fig.  8 ). It is clear from the expanded views (Fig.  8 b, d) that the relative fraction of PAGBs compared to the other boundaries in the microstructure is higher for rapidly austenitized (fine microstructure) materials than the starting (coarse microstructure) material, as the number fraction for misorientation angles in the range 19°–48° is higher for the rapidly austenitized microstructures than the starting microstructure. Further, the number fraction of PAGBs increased with number of rapid austenitizing cycles at 850 °C (Fig.  8 d). In contrast, the highest number fraction of PAGBs was observed at four rapid austenitizing cycles at 825 °C (Fig.  8 b). The misorientation angle distribution for multiple fields of view (FOVs) was plotted for the microstructures after four rapid austenitizing cycles at both the temperatures to check the reproducibility of these results, and the relative trend for different material conditions was the same, irrespective of the FOV considered. The details of EBSD scan areas for different microstructural conditions, which were used to plot the misorientation angle distributions shown in Fig.  8 , are presented in Table  5 . sections.heading: XRD Results
paragraphs: The processed XRD patterns for different heat treatment conditions are presented in Fig.  9 . The XRD patterns mostly show the peaks from  bct 1  martensite phase for the starting as well as the different rapidly austenitized and brine quenched microstructures. Two small peaks for  fcc  austenite are also observed for the material subjected to sixteen rapid austenitizing cycles at the lower temperature of 825 °C, and these austenite peaks were not observed for starting or other rapidly austenitized microstructures in this study. Fig. 9 XRD patterns for different material conditions of AF9628 steel. ( a ) Starting (coarse) microstructure, ( b ) rapidly austenitized at 825 °C for one cycle, ( c ) rapidly austenitized at 825 °C for four cycles, ( d ) rapidly austenitized at 825 °C for sixteen cycles, ( e ) rapidly austenitized at 850 °C for one cycle, ( f ) rapidly austenitized at 850 °C for four cycles, and ( g ) rapidly austenitized at 850 °C for sixteen cycles

sections.heading: Microhardness Results
paragraphs: The average of five microhardness measurements on each of the starting and the six rapidly austenitized microstructures are presented in Fig.  10 , where the error bars show one standard deviation (in both positive and negative directions) for each microstructure. The microhardness of microstructures after rapid austenitizing heat treatments (Fig.  4 ) was generally higher than that for microstructure before rapid austenitizing heat treatments (Fig.  3 ). One exception was the material after one rapid austenitizing cycle at 825 °C for which the microhardness was slightly lower than that for the material before rapid austenitizing heat treatment (Fig.  10 ). While increasing the number of rapid austenitizing cycles resulted in a more uniform distribution of finer PAGs (Fig.  4 ), the microhardness did not increase monotonically with the number of rapid austenitizing cycles at either 825 or 850 °C (Fig.  10 ). Fig. 10 Effects of microstructural refinement on microhardness in AF9628 steel. The error bars depict one standard deviation, in both positive and negative directions, from mean microhardness for different microstructural conditions. “RA” stands for rapid austenitizing

The microhardness was plotted against inverse of the square root of PAG size (Fig.  11 a) to assess how closely this material follows the Hall–Petch behavior [ 17 ,  18 ] if PAGB is considered the controlling microstructural feature for strengthening. The linear fit shows a low correlation coefficient (R 2  = 0.43), which suggests that the PAGBs are not the major contributors to strength in this material in these microstructural conditions. The block size was calculated from the EBSD data for starting and rapidly austenitized microstructures assuming block boundaries to be all the boundaries with misorientations greater than 5°. The microhardness was also plotted against inverse of the square root of block size (Fig.  11 b) to assess whether this material follows the Hall–Petch behavior [ 17 ,  18 ] if block boundary is considered the controlling microstructural feature for strengthening. The linear fit shows a lower correlation coefficient (R 2  = 0.22), which indicates that the block boundaries are also not the major contributors to strength in these microstructural conditions. Fig. 11 Effects of prior austenite grain size and block size on microhardness in AF9628 steel. ( a ) Hall–Petch plot of microhardness versus (average PAG size) −1/2  and ( b ) Hall–Petch plot of microhardness versus (average block size) −1/2 . The error bars depict one standard deviation, in both positive and negative directions, from mean microhardness for different microstructural conditions

sections.heading: Martensite to Austenite Phase Transformation on Rapid Heating
paragraphs: On rapidly heating the samples to a temperature above  A 3  from room temperature, there is a diffusionless revert transformation [ 19 ,  20 ] to austenite from martensite, as both austenite and martensite essentially have the same chemical composition. As a result, diffusion of carbon and other alloying elements is not needed for reverse transformation to austenite at 825 or 850 °C in the current study, which contrasts with the situation of equilibrium and metastable phases (i.e., ferrite and cementite) at room temperature that would necessitate diffusion of carbon and other alloying elements for austenitic transformation at a temperature above  A 3 . Further, the austenitic phase transformation in the two-phase (ferrite + austenite) region at a temperature between  A 1  and  A 3  (i.e., during intercritical anneal) may also require diffusion even if the room temperature microstructure is martensitic. As the diffusion of carbon and other alloying elements is not needed for direct phase transformation from martensite to austenite during rapid heating employed in the current study, this phase transformation occurs at a faster rate compared to the situations which would have required a diffusional phase transformation to occur. The revert transformation from martensite to austenite is exemplified by the EBSD maps (Fig.  4 ), which show newly nucleated PAGs even after short hold times (i.e., 30 s) at a temperature as low as 825 °C.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Microstructure Refinement
paragraphs: In this study, the PAG size as small as 2 μm was obtained via rapid austenitizing heat treatments on the starting microstructure with an initial PAG size of 77 μm (Table  3 ). This is a significant reduction in PAG size of 97%. The most rapid reduction in average PAG size occurred after one cycle (Fig.  6 ), which is consistent with the results of Furuhara, et al. [ 5 ].

Prior studies [ 1 ,  2 ] have reported increasingly finer microstructures with an increase in the number of rapid austenitizing cycles and the microstructural refinement eventually saturating with number of cycles. It was reported that no additional refinement occurred on cycling after three [ 5 ] or four [ 1 ] cycles. Further, these prior studies [ 1 ,  2 ,  5 ] reported essentially a uniform distribution of prior austenite grains after one or multiple rapid austenitizing cycles. In contrast, in the current research on AF9628 steel, a non-uniform distribution of newly nucleated prior austenite grains was observed after a low number (i.e., 1 or 4) of rapid austenitizing cycles. After one rapid austenitizing cycle, the finer prior austenite grains (Fig.  4 a, d) were primarily concentrated at the PAGBs of the microstructure before rapid austenitizing heat treatments (Fig.  3 ). However, a few finer prior austenite grains are disconnected from the PAGBs of starting microstructure and they result from nucleation of austenite grains within the prior austenite grains of starting microstructure at the temperature above  A 3  (i.e., 825 or 850 °C). Further, the number of prior austenite grains, which are disconnected from the PAGBs of starting microstructure, after one rapid austenitizing cycle is lower for 825 °C (Fig.  4 a) than for 850 °C (Fig.  4 d). This suggests a higher nucleation rate of austenite grains at 850 °C than at 825 °C, which is consistent with a higher thermodynamic driving force (i.e., Gibbs free energy change,  ΔG ) for martensite → austenite phase transformation at a higher temperature. This is further supported by a higher number of newly nucleated prior austenite grains at 850 °C than 825 °C (Fig.  7  and Table  4 ).

On subsequent rapid austenitizing cycles, the nucleation of additional austenite grains at 825 or 850 °C occurs and a short hold time of 30 s hinders the growth of newly nucleated austenite grains. The grain boundary pinning due to any carbides present in the microstructure at these temperatures slightly above  A 3  and the solute drag effect due to substitutional alloying elements in this steel also contribute to a limited growth of newly nucleated austenite grains. As a result, after four rapid austenitizing cycles, a higher fraction of microstructure consists of fine prior austenite grains (Fig.  4 b, e). The microstructure still consists of a few large prior austenite grains from the starting microstructure (Fig.  3 ) after four rapid austenitizing cycles at 825 °C (Fig.  4 b), and these large prior austenite grains are not observed after four rapid austenitizing cycles at a higher temperature of 850 °C (Fig.  4 e). This further suggests a higher nucleation rate of austenite grains at 850 °C than at 825 °C, which is consistent with the discussion above regarding the microstructures observed after one rapid austenitizing cycle at the two temperatures.

On subjecting the material to additional rapid austenitizing cycles, the above mechanism of refinement of prior austenite grains is repeated. As a result, after sixteen cycles, a uniform distribution of very fine prior austenite grains is observed for heat treatments at both the temperatures, 825 and 850 °C (Fig.  4 c, f). Any remnant prior austenite grains from the starting microstructure (Fig.  3 ) are not observed after such a large number of sixteen rapid austenitizing cycles at either temperature.

The PAG size is smaller for a rapid austenitizing temperature of 850 °C than 825 °C after one and four cycles (Table  3  and Fig.  6 ). However, the PAG size is larger for a rapid austenitizing temperature of 850 °C than 825 °C after sixteen cycles. The quantification of austenite nucleation sites after 30 s hold at 825 and 850 °C indicates a higher nucleation rate for 850 °C than 825 °C (Fig.  7  and Table  4 ). On the other hand, a higher growth rate of newly nucleated PAGs is expected at 850 °C than 825 °C. It appears that at a relatively low number of rapid austenitizing cycles (one to four), the nucleation rate is the dominating factor in determining the PAG size. As a result, microstructures with smaller PAG size are generated via rapid austenitizing at 850 °C than 825 °C after one to four cycles. In contrast, the growth rate becomes the major contributor to the PAG size at a high number of rapid austenitizing cycles (e.g., sixteen). Consequently, microstructure with a larger PAG size is generated via rapid austenitizing at 850 °C than 825 °C after sixteen cycles. Furuhara, et al. [ 5 ] also discuss that the saturated PAG size becomes larger at a higher temperature of rapid austenitizing heat treatments, which is consistent with our results after sixteen cycles (Table  3  and Fig.  6 ).

The results on material heated to the low austenitizing temperature of 825 °C, without employing rapid heating, and held at this temperature for 1 hour (Fig.  5 ) indicate that time at temperature, by itself, does not lead to PAG refinement in martensitic steels and rapid heating as well as short hold times in multiple cycles is crucial for grain refinement. This is expected as in the absence of rapid heating, the steel has to undergo diffusional phase transformation in the two-phase region (ferrite + austenite) with slower rates than diffusionless transformation (e.g., reverse austenitization) and more importantly, this sequence of diffusional phase transformation is not suitable to cause refinement of PAGs in microstructure.

The PAG size is the smallest for the material heat-treated with sixteen rapid austenitizing cycles at the lower temperature of 825 °C (Table  3  and Fig.  6 b), which can cause the highest retained austenite at room temperature in this material among the microstructures examined in this study. This is expected due to a higher stability of austenite during quenching of a steel with finer austenite grains, as the  M S -temperature is directly related to the austenite grain size before quenching from a temperature above  A 3  [ 21 ,  22 ]. This can explain the austenite peaks in XRD pattern from the material subjected to sixteen rapid austenitizing cycles at 825 °C and not from other rapidly austenitized materials in this study (Fig.  9 ).

sections.heading: Microstructure Evolution within Prior Austenite Grains
paragraphs: The size of microstructural features within the PAGs (e.g., packet size, block size, etc.) is generally reported in literature to be directly related to the PAG size [ 2 ,  23 ]. A plot of average block size versus average PAG size for the starting and the six rapidly austenitized microstructural conditions examined in current study (Fig.  12 a) appears to be consistent with literature data, as the linear fit has a high correlation coefficient (R 2  = 0.98). However, a consideration of only six rapidly austenitized microstructures (Fig.  12 b) shows that the linear fit has a very low correlation coefficient (R 2  = 0.05). In this context, it is important to note that the misorientation angle distributions indicate a higher fraction of PAGBs in comparison with the other microstructural boundaries for rapidly austenitized (fine) microstructures than the starting (coarse) microstructure. This would suggest that the number of martensite variants in unit volume of material does not increase proportionately with reduction in PAG size, as the microstructure is refined with rapid austenitizing heat treatments. This is consistent with Fig.  12 b, where no clear correlation was observed between the PAG size and block size in the six rapidly austenitized microstructures, as indicated by a very low correlation coefficient (R 2  = 0.05) for the linear fit. sections.heading: Strengthening Mechanisms
paragraphs: In the current study, the microhardness of examined steel did not increase monotonically with the number of rapid austenitizing cycles at either 825 or 850 °C (Fig.  10 ). This contrasts with the results of Hidalgo and Santofimia [ 2 ], who reported a monotonic increase in microhardness with number of rapid austenitizing cycles for martensitic microstructures in Fe−0.3C–1.6Si–3.5Mn steel. Our results also contrast the work of Grange [ 1 ], who postulated that the strength and toughness would increase with the number of rapid austenitizing cycles in martensitic or tempered martensitic microstructures.

The microstructural boundaries are generally believed to hinder the dislocation motion and cause strengthening in metals, commonly known as the Hall–Petch behavior [ 17 ,  18 ]. In the current study, the linear fits to microhardness versus inverse of square root of PAG size and inverse of square root of block size plots were observed to have slopes of 34.7 and 7.6, respectively (Fig.  11 ). These slopes are significantly smaller than the slopes of 92 for PAG size and 55.6 for block width reported by Hidalgo and Santofimia [ 2 ] for their material. In view of our results (Fig.  11 ), it appears that the microstructural boundaries do not offer significant strengthening in AF9628 and other strengthening mechanisms may be operative in this material in these microstructural conditions. In this context, it is interesting to note that Takaki, et al. reported a significant change in the microstructural feature sizes by varying the solution treatment temperature in an ultra-low carbon martensitic steel but did not observe a large difference in the yield behavior or strength for the widely different microstructures [ 24 ]. It was concluded that the strength is determined only by the mechanism of dislocation strengthening without any contributions by the boundaries in the microstructure (e.g., PAGB, packet boundary, or block boundary) in the ultra-low carbon martensitic steel [ 24 ]. Hao, et al. reported that the increase in microhardness in a ferritic/martensitic steel is caused primarily by the dislocation strengthening and not by the grain boundary strengthening [ 25 ], which is consistent with the study by Takaki, et al. [ 24 ]. It is possible that the dislocations and not the microstructural boundaries are the main contributors to strength in AF9628 steel examined in the current study.

Furthermore, the XRD results indicate that the amount of retained austenite increased with refinement of microstructure (Fig.  9 ). The differences in retained austenite amount in different microstructures can also contribute to the observed variations in the microhardness (Fig.  10  and  11 ), as austenite is known to be a softer phase than martensite [ 26 ,  27 ].

sections.heading: Summary and Conclusions
paragraphs: In this study, the microstructural refinement of a high strength martensitic steel was investigated with heat treatments alone, without recourse to mechanical deformation. The approach of rapid austenitizing was employed to refine the PAGs of starting martensitic microstructure. The effects of heat treatment temperature and number of rapid austenitizing cycles on the microstructural evolution were examined. The effects of microstructural refinement on microhardness were also assessed. The main conclusions of this study are summarized below: The PAGs of starting microstructure were successfully refined with rapid austenitizing heat treatments. The rapid austentizing was carried out at two temperatures, 825 and 850 °C. It was possible to refine the PAGs at both the temperatures. The PAG size as low as 2 μm was obtained from the initial microstructure with a PAG size of 77 μm. Thus, a reduction in PAG size of as high as 97% was obtained. The most rapid refinement was observed after one rapid austenitizing cycle. However, the distribution of PAG size in the microstructure was non-uniform. The small PAGs were distributed primarily at the PAGBs of starting microstructure, although a few PAGs were also observed in the interior of PAGs of starting microstructure. On increasing the number of rapid austenitizing cycles, the PAGs were further refined but at a decreasing rate in the subsequent cycles. However, the distribution of PAG size in microstructure became more uniform. The microstructural refinement is caused by the reverse transformation to austenite on rapid heating and hold at temperatures slightly above the  A 3  temperature. The nucleation and growth of reverted austenite control the microstructural evolution at different temperatures and at different numbers of rapid austenitizing cycles. The number of small PAGs after one cycle was higher for 850 °C than for 825 °C. The driving force for martensite → austenite phase transformation ( ΔG ) was higher at 850 °C than at 825 °C. Consequently, the nucleation rate of reverted austenite was substantially higher at 850 °C than at 825 °C, which resulted in a higher number of small PAGs after one cycle at 850 °C than at 825 °C. After one and four cycles, the average PAG size was smaller for a heat treatment temperature of 850 °C than for 825 °C. However, the trend reversed at 16 cycles, with the average PAG size being smaller for 825 °C than for 850 °C. The microstructures at different number of cycles depend on the nucleation and growth of reverted martensite at the two temperatures. At number of cycles ≤ 4, the microstructure has a smaller PAG size after heat treatment at 850 °C than at 825 °C as the nucleation rate is higher at 850 °C. As the number of cycles increases, even at the lower heat treatment temperature (with a lower nucleation rate) the nucleation of reverted austenite covers the entire microstructure including the interior of PAGs of the starting microstructure such that the microstructure consists of a uniform distribution of fine PAGs at sixteen cycles. At the lower temperature, growth rate is also lower. As a result, the reverted austenite grains do not grow to as large a size as at a higher temperature of 850 °C. Therefore, after 16 cycles, the PAG size is smaller for 825 °C than for 850 °C. The microhardness did not increase monotonically with the number of rapid austenitizing cycles. The linear fits to plots of microhardness versus inverse of square root of PAG size and block size had low correlation coefficients with R 2  of 0.43 and 0.22, respectively. This suggests that the PAGBs and block boundaries are not the primary contributors to strength in the examined material. The main contributors to strength in this material and these microstructural conditions could be the dislocation strengthening and the amount of retained austenite in microstructure.
